column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: In incomplete dominance, what does a heterozygous offspring look like?
column14: A blend that is in between the two parent traits
column16: Both parent traits showing side by side, like spots
column17: A brand-new trait unrelated to either parent
column28: In incomplete dominance neither allele fully wins, so the heterozygote is an in-between blend, like pink from red and white. Picking "both traits side by side" is the common mix-up: that describes codominance.
column29: Think of mixing red paint with white paint.

column9: In codominance, what does a heterozygous organism look like?
column15: Both traits show fully at the same time
column16: A blend that is in between the two traits
column28: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed, so both traits show at once, like red hairs and white hairs on a roan cow. A blend is incomplete dominance, which is the most common mix-up.
column29: Think of a checkered shirt: do the colors mix, or do they sit side by side?

column9: When neither allele is fully dominant and the heterozygote shows a blend of the two traits, the pattern is called ___ dominance.
column28: Incomplete dominance gives an in-between blend, like pink flowers from red and white parents. Writing "co" is the common mistake: codominance means both traits show, not a blend.
column29: Ask whether the dominant allele does a complete job of hiding the other one.

column9: When both alleles are fully expressed at the same time in a heterozygote, so both traits show, the pattern is called ___.
column28: Codominance means both alleles show, like type AB blood or roan cattle with red and white hairs. "Incomplete dominance" is the common wrong answer, but that is a blend.
column29: The prefix co- means together, like co-workers.

column9: How many different alleles for the ABO blood type gene exist in the human population?
column28: There are three alleles: A, B and O. Each person carries only two of them, which is why 2 is the common wrong answer.
column29: List the letters used to write blood type genotypes.

column9: Which genotype gives a person type O blood?
column28: O is recessive, so it only shows with two O alleles: OO. AO is type A and BO is type B, because A and B hide O.
column29: A recessive allele only shows when there are two copies of it.

column9: A person's blood type genotype is BO. What is their blood type?
column28: B is dominant over O, so BO is type B. Picking type O is the common mistake; one O allele is hidden by the B.
column29: Which allele in BO is recessive?

column9: A person with genotype AB has both A markers and B markers on their red blood cells, so their blood type is AB. Which pattern of inheritance explains this?
column28: Both alleles are fully expressed, so this is codominance. It is not incomplete dominance, because the A and B markers do not blend into something in between; both are present.
column29: Are the A and B markers blended together, or are both there?

column9: A class measures the heights of 500 students and graphs how many students are at each height. Height is controlled by many genes. Which graph shape should they expect?
column14: Two bars only: one for tall and one for short
column15: A bell-shaped curve with many in-between heights
column16: Three bars: tall, medium and short
column17: One bar, because everyone inherits the same height
column28: Many genes each add a little, so there are lots of in-between heights and a smooth bell curve. Two or three bars is the common mistake; that is what one gene with simple or incomplete dominance would give.
column29: With many genes adding up, how many different heights are possible?

column9: Red-green colorblindness is caused by a gene on which chromosome?
column28: The gene is on the X chromosome, which makes colorblindness a sex-linked trait. The Y is a common wrong pick, but the Y is small and does not carry this gene.
column29: Sex-linked traits ride on the larger of the two sex chromosomes.

column9: Which pair of sex chromosomes does a typical human male have?
column28: Males are XY and females are XX. Because males have only one X, a single recessive allele on it will show.
column29: A male gets one kind of sex chromosome from his mom and a different kind from his dad.

column9: Why is hemophilia, an X-linked recessive disorder, much more common in males than in females?
column14: Males have only one X, so one recessive allele is enough to cause it
column15: Males have two X chromosomes, so they get a double dose
column16: The Y chromosome carries a second copy of the allele
column17: Females cannot inherit genes on the X chromosome
column28: A male's single X has no partner to cover up a recessive allele, so one copy shows. A female needs two copies. The Y does not carry this gene, which is a common misunderstanding.
column29: Count how many X chromosomes a male has.

column9: In codominance, a heterozygous organism shows a blend of the two parent traits.
column28: False. A blend is incomplete dominance. In codominance both traits show fully at once, like red and white hairs on a roan cow.
column29: Blend, or both?

column9: In four o'clock flowers, red (RR) and white (WW) show incomplete dominance. What color is a four o'clock with the genotype RW?
column28: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is a blend, so red + white gives pink. Red with white spots would be codominance.
column29: Picture mixing red paint with white paint.

column9: When a red camellia is crossed with a white camellia, the offspring have petals with both red patches and white patches. Which pattern of inheritance is this?
column28: Both colors show separately on the same flower, so this is codominance. Incomplete dominance would make one in-between color, pink.
column29: Did the colors mix, or do both show?

column9: A chestnut (reddish-brown) horse is crossed with a cremello (cream-white) horse, and the foal is a palomino: a golden color in between the two parents. Which pattern best explains this?
column28: The foal's color is in between the parents' colors, a blend, which is incomplete dominance. Codominance would show separate chestnut hairs and cream hairs.
column29: Is the foal's coat a mix of the two colors, or a patchwork of both?

column9: Traits whose genes are carried on the X chromosome are called ___-linked traits.
column28: Genes on the X chromosome are sex-linked (also called X-linked). Colorblindness and hemophilia are examples.
column29: X and Y are called the ___ chromosomes.

column9: In the ABO blood type system, which allele is recessive?
column28: O is recessive to both A and B. A and B are codominant with each other, so neither one hides the other.
column29: Which blood type needs two copies of the same allele?

column9: Which of these is a sex-linked trait in humans?
column28: The colorblindness gene is on the X chromosome. ABO blood type is one gene with multiple alleles on a non-sex chromosome, and height and skin color are polygenic.
column29: Which trait is much more common in boys?

column9: For colorblindness, X^{B} is normal vision and X^{b} is colorblind. What best describes a woman with the genotype X^{B}X^{b}?
column14: She is homozygous for normal vision
column16: She has normal vision and is a carrier
column17: She has normal vision and cannot pass colorblindness to her children
column28: The dominant X^{B} gives her normal vision, but she still has one X^{b} that she can pass on, so she is a carrier. She is heterozygous, not homozygous.
column29: Which allele is dominant, and which allele does she still have?

column9: For colorblindness, X^{B} is normal vision and X^{b} is colorblind. Which genotype belongs to a colorblind male?
column28: Males are XY, so a colorblind male has one X^{b} and a Y. X^{b}X^{b} is a colorblind female, the common mix-up.
column29: A male's genotype always has a Y in it.

column9: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive: X^{H} = normal clotting and X^{h} = hemophilia. Match each genotype to the person it describes.
column14: X^{H}X^{H} :: Female with normal clotting who is not a carrier
column15: X^{H}X^{h} :: Female carrier with normal clotting
column28: Females have two X's: two normal alleles means not a carrier, one of each means a carrier, and two recessive alleles means hemophilia. Males have one X, so their single allele decides. A common mistake is calling X^{h}Y a carrier; males cannot be carriers.
column29: Start with the two genotypes that have a Y.

column9: Can a male be a carrier of an X-linked recessive trait like hemophilia?
column14: No. With only one X, he either has the trait or he does not
column15: Yes, every male is a carrier
column16: Only if his father has the trait
column17: Yes, if the allele is on his Y chromosome
column28: A carrier has a recessive allele hidden by a dominant one. A male has only one X, so nothing can hide his allele: he either has the trait or he doesn't. The Y does not carry this gene.
column29: To be a carrier, you need a second copy of the gene to hide the recessive allele.

column9: Human skin color comes in a smooth range of shades instead of a few separate types. Which pattern best explains this?
column14: A single gene with multiple alleles
column28: Skin color is controlled by several genes that add together, so there are many in-between shades. Multiple alleles of one gene, like ABO, still give only a few separate types.
column29: A smooth range usually means many genes are adding up.

column9: Match each pattern of inheritance to its description.
column14: Incomplete dominance :: The heterozygote is a blend of the two traits
column15: Codominance :: Both traits show fully at the same time
column16: Multiple alleles :: The gene has more than two versions in the population
column17: Polygenic trait :: Several genes add together to control one trait
column18: Sex-linked trait :: The gene is carried on the X chromosome
column28: Blend = incomplete dominance; both show = codominance; more than two versions = multiple alleles; many genes = polygenic; on the X = sex-linked. Mixing up incomplete dominance and codominance is the most common mistake.
column29: Match the ones you are surest of first. Poly- means many.

column9: Match each example to the pattern of inheritance it shows.
column14: Pink carnations from a red parent and a white parent :: Incomplete dominance
column15: Roan cattle with both red hairs and white hairs :: Codominance
column16: A blood type gene with A, B and O alleles :: Multiple alleles
column17: Human height, from very short to very tall :: Polygenic trait
column18: Hemophilia showing up mostly in boys :: Sex-linked trait
column28: Pink is a blend (incomplete dominance), roan shows both colors (codominance), three versions of one gene is multiple alleles, a smooth range of heights comes from many genes (polygenic), and a trait mostly in boys points to the X chromosome (sex-linked).
column29: Find the key clue in each example: a blend, both showing, three versions, a range, or mostly boys.

column9: Which of these is a possible genotype for a person with type A blood?
column28: A is dominant over O, so AO is type A (AA is also type A). BO is type B, OO is type O, and AB is type AB.
column29: The A allele must be there, and the other allele must not show.

column9: Select every genotype that gives type B blood. Select all that apply.
column28: BB and BO are both type B, because B hides O. AB is type AB, since A and B are codominant; picking AB is the common mistake.
column29: B must be present, and no other allele that shows can be present.

column9: A child has type O blood. What did the child inherit from each parent?
column14: An O allele from the mother only
column15: An A allele from one parent and a B allele from the other
column16: One O allele, from either parent
column17: An O allele from each parent
column28: Type O is OO, so each parent had to pass on an O. Getting an O from only one parent is the common mistake; then the other allele (A or B) would show.
column29: What genotype does every type O person have?

column9: For incomplete dominance and codominance, Punnett squares use two capital letters, like R and W, instead of R and r. Why?
column14: Because neither allele is dominant over the other
column16: Because the gene is on the X chromosome
column17: Because capital letters are easier to read
column28: A lowercase letter means recessive. In incomplete dominance and codominance neither allele is recessive, so both get capital letters.
column29: What does a lowercase letter usually tell you about an allele?

column9: What happens in a person who has hemophilia?
column14: They have an extra X chromosome
column15: Their blood does not clot normally
column16: They cannot tell red from green
column17: Their red blood cells are sickle-shaped
column28: Hemophilia is an X-linked disorder in which blood does not clot normally, so small cuts can bleed for a long time. Not telling red from green is colorblindness, the other common X-linked trait.
column29: Hemo- means blood.

column9: A female who has one normal allele and one recessive allele for an X-linked trait, but does not show the trait, is called a ___.
column28: She carries the recessive allele and can pass it on, but her dominant allele hides it. Males cannot be carriers because they have only one X.
column29: She can pass the allele to her children even though she doesn't show the trait. What do we call someone who transports something?

column9: In radishes, long (LL) and round (RR) show incomplete dominance. A long radish is crossed with a round radish. What will the offspring look like?
column16: All oval, in between long and round
column28: Every offspring is LR, and in incomplete dominance the heterozygote is a blend, so all are oval. "All long" is the common mistake; it treats long as fully dominant.
column29: Every offspring gets one L and one R. What does a blend of long and round look like?

column9: Human ABO blood type is a classic example of which pattern of inheritance?
column28: The ABO gene has three alleles (A, B and O), so it shows multiple alleles; A and B are also codominant. It is one gene, not many, so it is not polygenic.
column29: How many versions of the ABO gene exist?

column9: In incomplete dominance, how many different phenotypes can two alleles of one gene produce?
column28: The two homozygotes and the heterozygote each look different, for example red, pink and white. Answering 2 is the common mistake from simple dominance, where the heterozygote looks like the dominant parent.
column29: List the three possible genotypes and ask whether any two of them look the same.

column9: When you set up a Punnett square for an X-linked trait, what goes along the father's side?
column14: His X allele and his Y
column28: A father is XY, so his two entries are one X (with its allele) and a Y. Putting two X's on the father's side is the common setup mistake.
column29: Write out the father's sex chromosomes first.

column9: In a species of flower, red (RR) and white (WW) are codominant. What does a flower with the genotype RW look like?
column15: Red and white patches on the same flower
column28: In codominance both alleles show, so RW flowers have both red and white patches. Pink all over would be a blend, which is incomplete dominance.
column29: Codominant means both colors show. Do they mix?

column9: Which human sex chromosome is much smaller and carries far fewer genes?
column28: The Y is small and carries few genes, so most X-linked genes have no matching copy on the Y. That is why a male's single X allele always shows.
column29: Think of one as a long book and the other as a short pamphlet.

column9: Traits controlled by two or more genes are called ___ traits.
column28: Poly- means many, so polygenic means many genes. These traits show a smooth range, like height and skin color.
column29: The prefix for "many" is the same one in polygon.

column9: Put these steps in order for solving a complex inheritance cross.
column16: Count the boxes and write the ratios
column28: First decide the pattern so you know which letters to use, then write the parents' genotypes, fill the square, and count. Jumping to the square before naming the pattern leads to wrong letters, like using a lowercase letter for an allele that is not recessive.
column29: You can't write the genotypes until you know which kind of letters to use.

column9: In the genotype X^{B}Y, what does the Y tell you?
column14: The Y carries a recessive allele
column15: The Y carries a dominant allele
column17: The person is male, and the Y carries no allele for this gene
column28: The Y shows the person is male. The Y has no allele for this gene, so his X^{B} alone decides his phenotype. Thinking the Y carries a second allele is the common mistake.
column29: Is there a letter written on the Y?

column9: Select every trait that is polygenic. Select all that apply.
column28: Height and eye color come in many sizes or shades because several genes add together. ABO blood type is one gene with three alleles, hemophilia is one X-linked gene, and pink snapdragons come from one gene with incomplete dominance.
column29: Polygenic traits show a smooth range, not a few separate types.

column9: Suppose skin color is controlled by three genes (A, B and C), and each capital letter adds one unit of dark pigment. How many pigment-adding alleles does the genotype AaBBcc have?
column28: Count the capital letters: A, B and B make 3. A common mistake is counting only the different capital letters (A and B = 2); every copy adds pigment.
column29: Count every capital letter, including repeats.

column9: In a species of fish, blue (BB) and yellow (YY) show incomplete dominance, and BY fish are green. If a blue fish is crossed with a yellow fish, every offspring has the genotype ___.
column28: The blue parent can only pass on B and the yellow parent can only pass on Y, so every offspring is BY (green).
column29: What is the only allele each parent can pass on?

column9: A father can pass an allele on his X chromosome to his daughters.
column28: True. Every daughter gets her father's X, so she gets whatever allele is on it. Sons get his Y instead.
column29: Which sex chromosome does a father give to a daughter?

column9: In eggplants, purple (PP) and white (WW) show incomplete dominance, and PW eggplants are violet. Two violet eggplants are crossed. What percent of the offspring are expected to be purple?
column28: PW × PW gives 1 PP : 2 PW : 1 WW, so 1 box of 4 (25%) is purple. 75% is the common mistake: it treats purple as dominant, but here only PP is purple.
column29: Fill in the PW × PW square and count only the PP boxes.

column9: In carnations, RR flowers are red, RW flowers are pink and WW flowers are white. A pink carnation is crossed with a red carnation. Which offspring are expected?
column28: RW × RR gives RR, RR, RW, RW: half red and half pink. No white is possible because the red parent can only give R. 25/50/25 is the answer for pink × pink, the common mix-up.
column29: The red parent can only pass on R.

column9: In a beetle species, green (GG) and yellow (YY) show incomplete dominance, and GY beetles are yellow-green. Two yellow-green beetles are crossed and produce 200 offspring. About how many are expected to be yellow-green?
column28: GY × GY gives 1 GG : 2 GY : 1 YY, so half are GY: 1/2 × 200 = 100. Answering 150 is the common mistake; it treats green as dominant and uses 3/4.
column29: Find the fraction of GY boxes, then multiply by 200.

column9: The M and N blood group alleles are codominant: MM people are type M, NN people are type N, and MN people have both M and N markers. Two MN parents have children. What fraction of their children are expected to be type MN?
column28: MN × MN gives MM, MN, MN, NN, so 2 of 4 boxes (1/2) are MN. Answering 3/4 is the common mistake from simple dominance.
column29: Fill in the square and count only the boxes that have one M and one N.

column9: In a lizard species studied in a lab, orange (OO) and blue (BB) scales are codominant, and OB lizards have both orange scales and blue scales. An orange lizard is crossed with an OB lizard. Which offspring are expected?
column14: All with both orange and blue scales
column15: 50% orange and 50% with both orange and blue scales
column28: OO × OB gives OO, OO, OB, OB: half orange and half with both colors. No blue lizards are possible because the orange parent can only give O. A blended color would be incomplete dominance.
column29: The orange parent can only pass on O.

column9: A mother with type O blood (OO) and a father with type AB blood have children. Which blood types could their children have?
column14: Type AB or type O only
column16: Type A or type B only
column17: Types A, B, AB or O
column28: The square gives AO, AO, BO, BO, so every child is type A or type B. Many students pick AB or O because those are the parents' types, but no child here can match either parent.
column29: Each child gets one O from mom and either A or B from dad.

column9: Parents with the genotypes AA and BO have children. Which blood types could their children have?
column16: Types A, B, AB or O
column28: AA × BO gives AB, AO, AB, AO: type AB or type A. Type B is not possible because every child gets an A from the AA parent, and O is not possible for the same reason.
column29: The AA parent can only pass on one kind of allele.

column9: A parent with genotype AO and a parent with genotype BO have children. What percent of their children are expected to have type AB blood? Type the number only.
column28: AO × BO gives AB, AO, BO and OO, one box each, so 1 of 4 (25%) are type AB. Answering 0 is the common mistake; neither parent is AB, but each can pass on A or B.
column29: Put A and O across the top and B and O down the side.

column9: A colorblind father (X^{b}Y) and a mother with two normal-vision alleles (X^{B}X^{B}) have sons. Will any of their sons be colorblind?
column14: No, none of the sons are expected to be colorblind
column16: Yes, about half of the sons
column17: Yes, about one in four of the sons
column28: Sons get their Y from dad and their X from mom, and mom only has X^{B}. So every son is X^{B}Y with normal vision. The daughters, though, will all be carriers.
column29: Which parent gives a son his X chromosome?

column9: A colorblind mother (X^{b}X^{b}) and a father with normal vision (X^{B}Y) have children. What is expected for their sons?
column14: The sons will be carriers with normal vision
column15: All of the sons will be colorblind
column16: None of the sons will be colorblind
column17: Half of the sons will be colorblind
column28: Every son gets one of his mother's X chromosomes, and both of hers are X^{b}, so every son is X^{b}Y and colorblind. Males cannot be carriers, so "carriers with normal vision" is impossible for the sons.
column29: List the X chromosomes the mother can give.

column9: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is X-linked recessive. A carrier mother (X^{D}X^{d}) and an unaffected father (X^{D}Y) have a daughter. What is the chance the daughter has DMD?
column28: Every daughter gets her father's X^{D}, so no daughter can have DMD; half of the daughters are expected to be carriers. 50% is the chance for a son, and 25% is the chance for all children, which are the common mix-ups.
column29: What X does every daughter get from this father?

column9: A boy is colorblind, but both of his parents have normal vision. What must be true about his mother?
column17: Nothing; he got the colorblind allele from his father
column28: The boy's X came from his mother, so she must have an X^{b}. She has normal vision, so she is X^{B}X^{b}, a carrier. His father gave him a Y, so the allele could not come from dad.
column29: Which parent gave the boy his X chromosome?

column9: Identical twins have the same genes, but one twin grew up with poor nutrition and is 8 cm shorter than the other. What does this show about height?
column14: Height is controlled by only one gene
column16: The twins must have different genotypes
column17: The environment can affect a polygenic trait like height
column28: Identical twins share genotypes, so the difference came from the environment. Height is polygenic, and diet and health also shape how tall a person grows. Saying the twins have different genotypes is the common mistake.
column29: If the genes are identical, what else is different?

column9: Suppose skin color is controlled by three genes (A, B and C), and each capital letter adds one unit of dark pigment. Which genotype would have the darkest skin?
column28: Count the capital letters: AaBbCc = 3, AABbCC = 5, aaBBcc = 2 and AABbcc = 3. The most capitals means the most pigment, so AABbCC is darkest. Counting genes instead of capital letters is the common mistake.
column29: Count the capital letters in each genotype.

column9: Two pink-flowered plants are crossed. They produce 26 red, 51 pink and 24 white offspring. Which pattern of inheritance fits these results best?
column28: The results are close to 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, and pink is in between red and white. That is incomplete dominance. Simple dominance would give about 3 : 1 with no in-between color.
column29: Is pink in between the other two colors? What ratio do the numbers make?

column9: Two purple-flowered plants are crossed. They produce 76 purple and 24 white offspring, with no in-between colors. Which pattern fits these results best?
column28: 76 : 24 is about 3 : 1 with only two phenotypes, which is simple dominance from Pp × Pp. Incomplete dominance or codominance would give a third phenotype in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.
column29: How many phenotypes appeared, and what ratio is 76 : 24 close to?

column9: In simple dominance, a purple pea plant could be PP or Pp, so you can't tell its genotype by looking. In snapdragons with incomplete dominance, why can you tell a flower's genotype just by its color?
column14: The dominant allele always hides the other allele
column15: The gene is on the X chromosome
column17: Each genotype has its own phenotype, so red, pink and white each match one genotype
column28: RR is red, RW is pink and WW is white, so each color matches exactly one genotype. In simple dominance, PP and Pp look the same, which is why you can't tell them apart.
column29: Does any color in snapdragons come from two different genotypes?

column9: People with one normal hemoglobin allele and one sickle-cell allele make BOTH normal hemoglobin and sickle hemoglobin in their red blood cells. At the level of the proteins, which pattern is this?
column28: Both kinds of hemoglobin are made, so both alleles are fully expressed: codominance. Incomplete dominance would mean one in-between kind of hemoglobin, which is not what happens.
column29: Are both proteins made, or one blended protein?

column9: In a moth species, a black moth is crossed with a white moth, and the offspring have black and white speckled wings. A classmate says this is incomplete dominance. Which response is correct?
column14: The classmate is right, because the offspring look different from both parents
column15: The classmate is wrong; both colors show separately, so it is codominance
column16: The classmate is wrong; it is sex-linked because moths have sex chromosomes
column17: The classmate is right, because speckles are a blend of black and white
column28: Speckles mean both black and white show separately, which is codominance. Incomplete dominance would make a blended color, like gray wings. Looking different from both parents is true of both patterns, so it doesn't decide.
column29: What color would a true blend of black and white be?

column9: Two parents both have type A blood, but their child has type O blood. How is this possible?
column14: The child's blood type changed after birth
column15: Type A and type A always make type O
column16: Both parents are AO, and each passed an O allele to the child
column17: One parent must really be type O
column28: Type A can be AA or AO. If both parents are AO, each can pass on O, and the child is OO. The common mistake is thinking a type A parent can't carry O.
column29: Type A has two possible genotypes. Which one hides an O?

column9: One parent has genotype AB and the other has genotype AO. Select every blood type their children could have. Select all that apply.
column28: AB × AO gives AA, AO, AB and BO: types A, AB and B. Type O is impossible because the AB parent has no O allele to pass on.
column29: Fill in the square: A and B across the top, A and O down the side.

column9: Two parents both have type AB blood. What is the chance their child has type AB blood?
column28: AB × AB gives AA, AB, AB and BB, so 2 of 4 (50%) are type AB; the rest are type A or type B. 100% is the common mistake; the parents can each pass on A or B.
column29: Each parent can pass on A or B. Fill in all four boxes.

column9: Why can't a father pass an X-linked trait, like colorblindness, to his son?
column14: Sons never inherit any genes from their father
column15: The Y chromosome blocks the X allele from showing
column16: X-linked traits only pass from father to son
column17: A father gives his son a Y chromosome, not his X
column28: A son is a son because he got his father's Y. His X comes from his mother. Sons do get many genes from their father on other chromosomes, so saying sons get no genes from dad is the common overstatement.
column29: What makes a child a son instead of a daughter?

column9: In a three-gene skin color model, each capital letter adds one unit of dark pigment. Put these genotypes in order from lightest to darkest.
column28: Count the capitals: aabbcc = 0, AaBbcc = 2, AaBBCc = 4 and AABBCc = 5. Fewer capitals means lighter. Counting lowercase letters by mistake reverses the order.
column29: Count the capital letters in each genotype.

column9: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive. A carrier woman (X^{H}X^{h}) and a man with normal clotting (X^{H}Y) have 8 children. How many of the children are expected to have hemophilia?
column28: The square gives X^{H}X^{H}, X^{H}X^{h}, X^{H}Y and X^{h}Y. Only X^{h}Y has hemophilia, so 1 of 4 children: 1/4 × 8 = 2. Answering 4 is the common mistake; half of the sons is not half of all the children.
column29: Find the fraction of ALL four boxes with hemophilia, then multiply by 8.

column9: In fruit flies, red eyes (X^{R}) are dominant over white eyes (X^{r}). A red-eyed female carrier (X^{R}X^{r}) is crossed with a red-eyed male (X^{R}Y), and they produce 400 offspring. About how many are expected to have white eyes?
column28: The square gives X^{R}X^{R}, X^{R}X^{r}, X^{R}Y and X^{r}Y. Only X^{r}Y is white-eyed, so 1/4 × 400 = 100, and all of them are males. Answering 0 is the common mistake from forgetting the mother carries X^{r}.
column29: Only one of the four boxes has no X^{R}.

column9: Match each pair of parents to the blood types their children could have.
column16: AO × OO :: Type A or type O
column18: AO × BB :: Type AB or type B
column28: AA × BB always gives AB. OO × OO always gives O. AO × OO gives AO or OO. BB × OO always gives BO, which is type B. AO × BB gives AB or BO. Forgetting that BO is type B, not type O, is the common mistake.
column29: For each pair, list the alleles each parent can pass on.

column9: A gene for coat color has four different alleles in a population of rabbits. How many alleles for this gene does each rabbit carry?
column28: Every rabbit has two copies of each gene, one from each parent, no matter how many alleles exist in the population. Answering 4 is the common mistake; the population has four, but one rabbit has only two.
column29: How many copies of each gene do you get from your parents?

column9: In shorthorn cattle, red (RR) and white (WW) are codominant, and RW calves are roan. A roan bull is bred with many roan cows, and 64 calves are born. About how many calves are expected to be red?
column28: RW × RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW, so 1/4 are red: 1/4 × 64 = 16. Answering 48 is the common mistake; it treats red as dominant and uses 3/4.
column29: Only RR calves are red. What fraction of the square is RR?

column9: Colorblindness is X-linked recessive. Which parents could have a daughter who is colorblind?
column14: A carrier mother (X^{B}X^{b}) and a colorblind father (X^{b}Y)
column15: A carrier mother (X^{B}X^{b}) and a father with normal vision (X^{B}Y)
column16: A colorblind mother (X^{b}X^{b}) and a father with normal vision (X^{B}Y)
column17: A mother with two normal alleles (X^{B}X^{B}) and a colorblind father (X^{b}Y)
column28: A colorblind daughter is X^{b}X^{b}, so she needs an X^{b} from BOTH parents. Only a carrier mother and a colorblind father can each give X^{b}. A father with normal vision always gives X^{B} to his daughters.
column29: A daughter gets one X from each parent. Both have to be X^{b}.

column9: A child has type O blood, and the mother has type A blood. Which blood type could the father NOT have?
column28: The child is OO, so the father must have passed on an O. Type A (AO), type B (BO) and type O (OO) fathers can all give O, but a type AB father has no O allele.
column29: Which blood type has no O allele to give?

column9: In fruit flies, red eyes (X^{R}) are dominant over white eyes (X^{r}). A white-eyed female (X^{r}X^{r}) is crossed with a red-eyed male (X^{R}Y), and they produce 100 offspring. About how many are expected to have white eyes?
column28: Every daughter gets X^{R} from dad and X^{r} from mom, so all daughters are red-eyed carriers. Every son gets X^{r} from mom and Y from dad, so all sons are white-eyed. About half the flies are sons: 50. Answering 0 is the common mistake from thinking red is dominant for everyone.
column29: Do the sons and the daughters separately.

column9: A woman with type AB blood and a man with genotype BO have children. What percent of their children are expected to have type A blood? Type the number only.
column28: AB × BO gives AB, AO, BB and BO: type AB, type A, type B and type B. Only AO is type A, so 1 of 4 = 25%. Answering 0 is the common mistake; AO is type A even though the father is not.
column29: Fill in the square, then decide the blood type of each box.

column9: In cats, a gene for orange or black fur is on the X chromosome. A cat needs one orange allele AND one black allele to have the orange-and-black patches of a calico. Why are nearly all calico cats female?
column14: The Y chromosome carries the black allele
column15: Calico is caused by many genes adding together
column16: Females have two X chromosomes, so they can carry one orange and one black allele
column17: Males have two X chromosomes, so the colors cancel out
column28: A female (XX) can have one orange allele and one black allele, so both colors show. A typical male (XY) has only one X, so he is either orange or black, not both. The Y does not carry this gene.
column29: How many copies of an X-linked gene can a male have?

column9: A baby has type AB blood, and the mother has type A blood. Which man could be the baby's father?
column14: A man with type A blood (AA)
column15: A man with type O blood
column16: A man with type A blood (AO)
column17: A man with type B blood
column28: The type A mother can give only A or O, so the baby's B allele must come from the father. Of these choices, only the type B man has a B allele (a type AB man could also be the father).
column29: Which allele in the baby could NOT have come from the mother?

column9: A woman with normal vision has a father who is colorblind. She has children with a man who has normal vision. What is the chance that their son will be colorblind?
column28: Her father gave her his only X, which is X^{b}, so she is a carrier (X^{B}X^{b}). Each son gets one of her X's, so 50% of sons are expected to be colorblind. 25% is the chance for all children, not just sons.
column29: First figure out her genotype from her father, then do the square.

column9: A woman has hemophilia (X^{h}X^{h}). What must be true about her father?
column15: He is a carrier but has normal clotting
column17: There is no way to know
column28: She got one X from each parent, so one X^{h} came from her father. A father has only one X, so he must be X^{h}Y and have hemophilia. Males cannot be carriers, so he can't be a carrier with normal clotting.
column29: A daughter always gets her father's only X.

column9: In eggplants, PP is purple, PW is violet and WW is white. A breeder crosses an eggplant of unknown genotype with a white eggplant and gets about half violet and half white offspring. What is the unknown parent's genotype?
column28: PW × WW gives PW, PW, WW, WW: half violet and half white, which matches. PP × WW would give all violet, and WW × WW would give all white.
column29: Try each possible genotype in a square with WW and see which matches.

column9: In snapdragons, RR is red, RW is pink and WW is white. A grower wants a greenhouse full of ONLY pink snapdragons. Which cross should she make?
column28: RR × WW gives RW in every box, so 100% pink. Crossing two pinks (RW × RW) is the common choice, but it gives only 50% pink, with red and white too.
column29: Which cross gives the same genotype in all four boxes?

column9: The M and N blood group alleles are codominant (MM = type M, MN = type MN, NN = type N). A mother with type MN has a child with type N. Select every genotype the father could have. Select all that apply.
column28: The type N child is NN, so the father must have passed on an N. MN and NN fathers both have an N to give; an MM father does not.
column29: What allele did the child have to get from the father?

column9: In a two-gene model of skin color, each capital letter (A or B) adds one unit of dark pigment. A parent with genotype AABB is crossed with a parent with genotype aabb. What will their children be like?
column14: Half dark like AABB and half light like aabb
column15: All as dark as the AABB parent
column17: All AaBb, with a medium shade
column28: The AABB parent can only pass on AB and the aabb parent can only pass on ab, so every child is AaBb with 2 capitals: a medium shade. The 1 : 2 : 1 pattern is the common mistake from a one-gene cross.
column29: What is the only combination each parent can pass on?

column9: In a two-gene skin color model, each capital letter adds one unit of pigment. Two parents are both AaBb. In the 16-box Punnett square for this cross, how many boxes have exactly two capital letters?
column28: Each parent can pass on AB, Ab, aB or ab. Counting capitals in the 16 boxes gives 1 box with 0, 4 with 1, 6 with 2, 4 with 3 and 1 with 4. The 6 boxes with two capitals are AaBb (4 boxes), AAbb (1) and aaBB (1). Counting only the AaBb boxes (4) is the common mistake.
column29: Each parent's possible combinations are AB, Ab, aB and ab. Remember AAbb and aaBB also have two capitals.

column9: A cross between two plants with red-and-white spotted flowers produces 30 red, 62 red-and-white spotted and 28 white offspring. A student says red must be dominant. Which response is correct?
column14: No. The spotted offspring show both colors, so red and white are codominant; with red dominant, about 3/4 would be red and none spotted
column15: Yes, because red shows up in two of the three phenotypes
column16: No, because the trait must be sex-linked
column17: Yes, because there are more red offspring than white
column28: The 1 : 2 : 1 ratio with a third phenotype showing both colors points to codominance. If red were dominant, you'd see about 3 red : 1 white and no spotted flowers. Small differences like 30 vs 28 are just chance.
column29: What ratio would a dominant red give, and would there be any spotted flowers?

column9: In rabbits, coat color has four alleles with a dominance order: full color (C) > chinchilla (c^{ch}) > Himalayan (c^{h}) > albino (c). A chinchilla rabbit (c^{ch}c^{h}) is crossed with a Himalayan rabbit (c^{h}c). What percent of the babies are expected to be Himalayan?
column28: The square gives c^{ch}c^{h} (chinchilla), c^{ch}c (chinchilla), c^{h}c^{h} (Himalayan) and c^{h}c (Himalayan). Two of four boxes are Himalayan: 50%. Calling c^{h}c albino is the common mistake; Himalayan is dominant over albino.
column29: Put c^{ch} and c^{h} across the top and c^{h} and c down the side, then use the dominance order.

column9: A man with type B blood and a woman with type A blood have a child with type O blood. What are the parents' genotypes?
column28: The child is OO, so each parent must have passed on an O. The only genotypes for type B and type A that carry an O are BO and AO.
column29: What did the type O child need from each parent?

column9: In fruit flies, red eyes (X^{R}) are dominant over white eyes (X^{r}). A red-eyed carrier female (X^{R}X^{r}) is crossed with a white-eyed male (X^{r}Y). Select every statement that is true about the expected offspring. Select all that apply.
column14: About half of the daughters have white eyes
column15: About half of the sons have white eyes
column16: All of the daughters have red eyes
column17: None of the sons have white eyes
column18: Every red-eyed daughter is a carrier (X^{R}X^{r})
column28: The square gives X^{R}X^{r} and X^{r}X^{r} daughters, and X^{R}Y and X^{r}Y sons. So half of each sex is white-eyed, and every red-eyed daughter got X^{r} from dad, making her a carrier. Thinking daughters are always protected is the common mistake; here dad gives X^{r}.
column29: Write dad's X^{r} and Y down the side, and mom's X^{R} and X^{r} across the top.

column9: A colorblind grandfather (X^{b}Y) has a colorblind grandson through his daughter. The grandmother and the grandson's father both have normal vision and carry no colorblind allele. Put the steps in order.
column14: The daughter passes her X^{b} to her son
column15: The grandfather passes his X^{b} to his daughter
column17: The daughter is a carrier (X^{B}X^{b}) with normal vision
column28: The grandfather gives his only X to every daughter, so she is a carrier with normal vision. She then passes X^{b} to her son, who has no second X to hide it. This is why X-linked traits often seem to skip a generation.
column29: Start with the grandfather, and remember a daughter always gets her father's X.

column9: Which pair of parents could NOT have a child with type O blood?
column28: A type O child needs an O from each parent. The AA parent has no O allele to give, so AA × BO cannot have a type O child. Every other pair has an O in both parents.
column29: Check whether both parents in each pair have an O.

column9: Height is polygenic. Two parents of medium height have a child who grows taller than both of them. How is this possible?
column14: The child must have a dominant height allele that neither parent has
column15: Height is sex-linked, so sons are always taller
column16: This is impossible; a child can't be taller than both parents
column17: The child inherited more height-adding alleles, across many genes, than either parent has
column28: Each parent passes on a random mix of their alleles for many height genes. By chance a child can get more of the height-adding alleles than either parent has. A child can't get an allele neither parent has (barring a new mutation), so a "dominant allele neither parent has" is not the explanation.
column29: Think of each parent passing on a random handful of their alleles.

column9: A cross between two heterozygous parents gives three different phenotypes in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio. Which patterns of inheritance could explain this? Select all that apply.
column28: In both incomplete dominance and codominance the heterozygote has its own phenotype, so a heterozygous cross gives 1 : 2 : 1. Simple dominance gives only two phenotypes (3 : 1), and many genes give a smooth range, not three classes.
column29: In which patterns does the heterozygote look different from both homozygotes?

column9: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is X-linked recessive. A boy has DMD. His mother does not have DMD, but her brother (the boy's uncle) does. Neither of the mother's parents has DMD. Who most likely passed the DMD allele to the boy's mother?
column14: Her mother (the boy's grandmother), who is a carrier
column28: The grandfather does not have DMD, so his only X is normal. The uncle and the boy's mother both had to get their DMD allele from the grandmother, who must be a carrier. The boy's father gave the boy a Y, and he had no part in the alleles the mother inherited. Picking the grandfather is the common mistake; an unaffected male cannot carry a hidden DMD allele.
column29: The grandfather is unaffected. What does that tell you about the X he gave his daughter?

column9: Two babies were mixed up in a hospital. Baby 1 has type O blood, and Baby 2 has type B blood. Couple X are both type AB. Couple Y are a type O mother and a type A father. Which baby belongs to Couple X?
column16: Either baby could belong to Couple X
column17: Neither baby could belong to Couple X
column28: AB × AB can give type A, AB or B, but never O, so Couple X's baby is Baby 2. Couple Y (O × A) can only give type A or type O, so Baby 1 belongs to them. Thinking AB parents can have any blood type is the common mistake.
column29: List the blood types each couple can and can't have.

column9: In shorthorn cattle, red (RR) and white (WW) are codominant, and RW calves are roan, with red and white hairs mixed. A farmer has a herd of white cows and wants every calf to be roan. Which bull should she use?
column28: Every white cow gives W, so the bull must give R every time. Only an RR bull does that, making every calf RW (roan). A roan bull would give only 50% roan calves, which is the common choice.
column29: Which bull can only pass on R?

column9: In corn, a plant with 10 cm ears is crossed with a plant with 20 cm ears. The offspring all have ears about 15 cm long. When those offspring are crossed with each other, the next generation has ears of every length from 10 to 20 cm, with most near 15 cm. Which pattern best explains this?
column14: Incomplete dominance of a single gene
column28: A smooth range of lengths with most in the middle comes from many genes adding together. One gene with incomplete dominance would give only three lengths (10, 15 and 20 cm) in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, which is the common wrong answer.
column29: How many different ear lengths would a single gene give?

column9: A man with type AB blood and normal vision (X^{B}Y) has children with a woman who has type O blood and is a carrier for colorblindness (X^{B}X^{b}). Which child is possible?
column14: A colorblind son with type B blood
column15: A son with type AB blood
column16: A son with type O blood
column17: A colorblind daughter with type A blood
column28: Blood type: AB × OO gives only AO (type A) or BO (type B), so type O and type AB children are impossible. Vision: every daughter gets dad's X^{B}, so no daughter is colorblind, but a son can get mom's X^{b}. So a colorblind son with type B blood (BO) is possible.
column29: Work the blood type and the vision separately, then check each choice against both.
